abstract.p: The mRNA-lipid nanoparticles (mRNA@LNPs) offer a novel opportunity to treat targets previously considered undruggable. Although antibody conjugation is crucial for enhancing the specificity, delivery efficiency, and minimizing the toxicity of mRNA therapeutics, current chemical conjugation methods are complex and produce heterogeneous particles with misoriented antibodies. In this work, we introduce a chemical-free approach to functionalize mRNA@LNPs with antibodies, mimicking protein corona formation for targeted mRNA delivery. By fusing apolipoprotein to the Fc domain of a targeting antibody, we enabled the antibody to spontaneously display on the surface of mRNA@LNPs without altering the existing LNP process or employing complex chemical conjugation techniques. We demonstrated precise protein expression using trastuzumab-bound mRNA@LNPs, facilitating specific mRNA expression in HER2-positive cancer cells. mRNA was efficiently delivered to the tumor site after intravenous administration. While the control LNPs lacking targeting antibodies caused acute liver toxicity, trastuzumab-displayed LNPs showed no systemic toxicity. The tumor-specific delivery of p53 tumor suppressor mRNA led to the complete regression of cancer cells. Thus, apolipoprotein fusion enables a straightforward and scalable production of antibody-functionalized mRNA@LNPs, offering significant therapeutic potential in gene therapy.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The recent success of mRNA@lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines against COVID-19 highlights their potential for treating various diseases.1−6 These mRNA-based therapies have shown significant promise in personalized cancer vaccines,7−10 the expression of immunomodulatory factors,11,12 and the upregulation of tumor suppressor genes.13−15 This success is because LNPs serve as robust carriers for mRNA by protecting it from biological degradation and facilitating cellular uptake.16−19 However, challenges such as nonspecific delivery and unintended organ accumulation persist, posing risks like liver toxicity and compromising therapeutic efficacy.20−22

Targeting strategies for mRNA@LNPs fall into two categories: passive and active targeting. Passive targeting leverages the physical and chemical properties of LNPs, along with the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect observed in tumors, which promotes their accumulation in specific tissues.23 This approach relies on the natural distribution of particles within the body and high-throughput screening of various formulations to assess organ and tissue distribution. However, passive targeting suffers from lower specificity, which may result in less efficient delivery to target cells and an increased risk of off-target effects and systemic toxicity. In contrast, active targeting involves modifying the surface of nanoparticles with specific ligands or antibodies to bind to receptors on target cells. Antibody conjugation is considered crucial for the effectiveness of mRNA@LNP therapeutics beyond vaccines, ensuring maximal therapeutic impact and minimal toxicity. For example, active targeting of mRNA@LNPs to T cells using antibodies against CD3, CD4, or CD5 facilitates in vivo T cell transfection to generate CAR T cells.24−26 This approach offers several advantages, including the absence of genomic integration, lower production costs, and reduced toxicity due to the transient nature of the mRNA payload. Another emerging application of mRNA@LNPs is in vivo genome editing, particularly using CRISPR-based technologies.27,28 However, the success of these methods relies on the precise delivery of mRNA payloads to target cells, avoiding irreversible genomic changes in nontarget cells. Therefore, antibody conjugation to mRNA@LNPs for enhanced cell-specific delivery is critical for the future applications of this versatile platform.

However, significant challenges remain in antibody conjugation to mRNA@LNPs. The process is complex, typically involving polyethylene glycol (PEG) lipids and bio-orthogonal conjugation techniques that use toxic chemicals such as dibenzocyclooctyne or maleimide.20,29 Achieving high conjugation efficiency is difficult due to the multistep process, often resulting in low yields and heterogeneous LNP populations. The conjugation methods involving chemicals require extensive purification steps. Moreover, conventional conjugation methods are time-consuming and labor-intensive, limiting scalability.30,31 Furthermore, PEG shedding, where PEG molecules detach from LNP surfaces in a biological environment, can cause antibodies to dislodge.32 To address these challenges, a novel approach called Anchored Secondary scFv Enabling Targeting (ASSET) has been developed.33,34 This method uses a secondary single-chain variable fragment (scFv) as an anchor on the LNP surface, which binds the Fc region of the primary antibody. ASSET offers several advantages, including preserving antibody integrity and ensuring correct orientation and functionality. However, ASSET still faces challenges, such as manufacturing complexity, potential immunogenicity due to the use of E. coli membrane-derived micelles, stability concerns, and the need for customization.25,35

In response to these limitations, we developed a novel, chemical-free approach to attach antibodies to LNPs, ensuring proper orientation and simplifying the conjugation process. This method involves fusing a targeting antibody to an apolipoprotein, creating the “Grab Antibody” (GrAb), inspired by the protein corona formation observed upon contact with blood.36 Apolipoprotein A1 (ApoA1), integral to high-density lipoproteins (HDL), are known for their lipid-binding properties and are established as safe drug carriers.37 Due to its strong binding (∼200 kCal/mol) to HDL, ApoA1 enables GrAb to securely adhere to LNPs, forming a hard protein corona that prevents antibody stripping and remains stable for hours to days.38−41 Furthermore, by covering the LNP surface, GrAb is expected to prevent inadvertent delivery by serum proteins, facilitating targeted delivery to specific cells. To test the therapeutic potential of the target-specific mRNA@LNP generated with GrAb, we explored whether the p53 gene, known as the “guardian of the genome”, could be effectively targeted to cancer cells through intravenous injection. Mutations in p53 are present in approximately half of all human cancers, making it a prime target for therapeutic intervention.42−44 p53 gene therapy aims to restore the gene’s normal function, thereby reactivating its tumor-suppressing capabilities.45,46 We utilized trastuzumab, a human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-targeting antibody, to introduce mRNA encoding p53 into HER2-positive cancer cells.47,48 The antibody-guided active mRNA delivery system was biochemically characterized and subsequently evaluated for efficacy in aggressive tumor models. The novel delivery system demonstrated efficient tumor inhibition and a significant reduction in off-target toxicity by achieving precise tumor targeting through specific binding to the receptor overexpressed on cancer cells. This study is the first to report the GrAb technology and the antibody-guided targeted delivery of p53 mRNA@LNP, marking a significant advancement in therapeutic strategies for cancer treatment.

sec.title: Construction and Characterization of the GrAb Platform
sec.p: In this study, we developed a chemical-free method for functionalizing mRNA@LNPs with antibodies. Our approach utilized the fusion protein GrAb, which included two functional domains: a targeting antibody domain and an apolipoprotein domain (Figure 1A). The apolipoprotein component of GrAb was fused to promote the formation of a protein corona on the surface of LNPs, effectively “grabbing” the LNPs and enhancing their specificity. To achieve this, we constructed two plasmids encoding the N-terminal signal sequence followed by the heavy chain of the antibody and an apolipoprotein, as well as the light chain of the antibody with an N-terminal signal sequence (Figure 1B, please refer to the Materials and Methods section for detailed methodology). Trastuzumab was used as the antibody to target HER2, while ApoA1 and ApoE3, key components of protein corona on LNP, were chosen to construct the GrAbs. GrAbs were expressed in ExpiCHO cells, yielding approximately 190 mg/L for ApoA1 and 35 mg/L for ApoE3 after purification (Figure 1C). A simple incubation of LNPs with GrAb antibodies at 37 °C for 30 min enabled efficient display of antibodies on the LNP surface through apolipoprotein-mediated interaction (Figure 1D). This approach enabled LNP functionalization with antibodies by controlling the lipid-to-protein molar ratio (LP ratio), which determines the amount of antibody displayed on the LNP surface. For instance, an LP ratio of 100,000:1 indicates that one GrAb protein molecule is mixed with 100,000 lipid molecules.

sec.p: Next, we aimed to optimize the incubation ratio of GrAb by introducing it to LNPs at various LP ratios (from 500 to 100,000:1). In the case of ApoA1-mediated assembly, we observed a slight increase in size from 132 ± 3 nm to 140 ± 3 nm at an LP ratio 10,000:1, with a negligible change in the polydispersity index (PDI) value. However, ApoE3-mediated assembly resulted in a size increase to 173 ± 6 nm at an LP ratio of 10,000:1 or higher, except at 100,000:1. Additionally, we noted a decrease in mRNA encapsulation efficiency as the ratio of GrAb increased for both ApoA1 and ApoE3 (Figure 1E). These findings are consistent with previous reports indicating that apolipoproteins can reconstitute the surface of LNPs, potentially leading to mRNA leakage. Nevertheless, for ApoA1, we observed no difference in encapsulation efficiency from an LP ratio of 10,000:1 onward, suggesting minimal mRNA leakage (Figure 1F). The encapsulation efficiency, size, and PDI values remained consistent irrespective of the mRNA type (Figure S1).

To assess the stability of GrAb-LNPs across various LP ratios, we stored them at 4 °C for 7 days and monitored any size changes. At the highest LP ratio of 500:1, both ApoA1- and ApoE3-mediated reactions resulted in size increases due to protein-mediated aggregation. At lower LP ratios, ApoA1 remained stable in size after a week, whereas ApoE3-mediated assembly led to size increases except for the 100,000:1 ratio (Figure 1G). To assess the serum stability of GrAb-LNPs at an LP ratio of 10,000:1, we incubated LNPs and GrAb-LNPs with 50% mouse serum. The particles retained their size after 72 h of incubation (Figure S2).

To confirm the stable incorporation of GrAb onto LNPs via ApoA1-mediated assembly, we performed size-exclusion chromatography (SEC; Figure 1H). Samples of free GrAb protein, bare LNPs, and Trastuzumab GrAb-conjugated LNPs (HerLNPs) were loaded onto the column, and the early fractions corresponding to larger particles (F1–F9) were collected. SDS-PAGE analysis of these fractions showed that GrAb proteins were exclusively present in the fractions containing HerLNPs. In contrast, no protein bands were detected in the fractions from bare LNPs or free GrAb samples, confirming that GrAb is specifically and stably incorporated into the LNPs. After incubation of LNPs with Cy5-labeled trastuzumab or its GrAb at an LP ratio of 10,000:1, fractions containing antibody-bound LNPs were pooled to analyze the ratio of residual to initial Cy5 fluorescence, which showed that most of the GrAb was incorporated into the LNPs (Figure 1I). Notably, under 100% serum and continuous shaking conditions to simulate the physiological environment in plasma, GrAb proteins remained stably attached to the LNPs for up to 12 h, with only a modest detachment of 29.60% observed at 24 h. To further confirm these findings, we conducted in vivo experiments using fluorescence-labeled GrAbs (APC) and LNPs (FITC) to track their stability and colocalization over time. Serum collected from mice at various time points postinjection were analyzed via flow cytometry, revealing consistent colocalization of LNP and GrAb signals for up to 12 h. At 24 h, the modest detachment observed (26.77 ± 5.22%) corroborated the in vitro trends (Figure S3). Subsequently, we determined the number of GrAb molecules bound to the surface of LNPs by measuring particle number and GrAb quantity. The number of particles was assessed using nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), while GrAb molecules in LNPs were quantified using a DC protein assay kit. At an LP ratio of 10,000:1, approximately 69 GrAb molecules were displayed on the surface of the LNPs (Figure 1J). Assuming that the GrAbs are evenly distributed, they form a roughly hexagonal pattern on the surface of the LNP, with the average distance between GrAbs on the surface of the 135 nm diameter LNP being approximately 30.97 nm. Given that the antibody is approximately 14 nm thick, this spacing suggests that the GrAb enabled high-density antibody loading into the LNP. When the size and shape of the HerLNP were compared to the nude LNP by cryo-TEM imaging, both LNPs and HerLNPs were spherical in shape and similar in size (Figure 1K).

Taken together, these results indicate that the apolipoprotein of a GrAb effectively mediates association with the LNPs. This capability facilitates the rapid production of LNPs designed for targeted delivery, leveraging the specificity of the antibody domain of the GrAb for precise cellular targeting.

sec.title: Receptor-Mediated Cellular Targeting of GrAb-LNPs
sec.p: We further investigated whether HerLNPs can selectively bind to their target HER2-positive cancer cells. The specificity of GrAb-LNPs labeled with DiD for HER2 was assessed in both HER2-negative MDA-MB-231 cells and HER2-positive SK-OV-3, SK-BR-3, MDA-MB-453, and BT-474 cancer cell lines (Figure S4). Then, we evaluated cellular uptake at different LP ratios, observing a gradual increase in uptake efficiency as the LP ratio decreased, reaching a maximum at 1,000:1 (Figure S5). However, due to insufficient mRNA encapsulation efficiency at LP ratios below 10,000:1 (Figure 1F), we selected a 10,000:1 LP ratio for subsequent in vivo and in vitro experiments. For comparison, we included isotype LNPs (IsoLNPs) in addition to the control LNPs without GrAb (ConLNPs). IsoLNPs are engineered with isotype-control of GrAb that do not bind to HER2 and differ from HerLNPs only in the variable domain that targets the antigen (Figure 2A). A significant increase in DiD fluorescence intensity was observed specifically in HER2-positive cancer cell lines (SK-OV-3, SK-BR-3, MDA-MB-453, and BT-474) when treated with HerLNPs (Figures 2B and S6A) in contrast to the results obtained with ConLNPs and IsoLNPs. However, in the MDA-MB-231 cell line, there was no discernible difference in DiD fluorescence intensity between cells treated with ConLNPs, IsoLNPs, or HerLNPs (Figure S6B). Preblocking of the HER2 receptor with an antibody in the SK-OV-3 cell line abolished the differential uptake of HerLNPs, resulting in fluorescence intensities comparable to those observed in MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 2C). Furthermore, the binding affinity of HerLNPs persisted even after 24 h of incubation in 50% of mouse serum, indicating no loss of targeting ability under biological conditions (Figure 2D).

sec.p: The HER2-dependent cellular uptake of mRNA by HerLNPs was confirmed using Cy5-labeled firefly luciferase (Fluc) mRNA-loaded LNPs, visualized by confocal fluorescence microscopy in SK-OV-3 cells (Figures 2E and S7). HerLNPs showed rapid intracellular mRNA uptake compared to ConLNPs and IsoLNPs. This uptake was significantly inhibited when the receptor was blocked by preincubating the cells with anti-HER2 antibodies (Figure 2F). To further evaluate the mRNA release profile, endosomal escape was monitored using calcein, which initially colocalizes with mRNA within endosomes upon cellular internalization but separates following successful endosomal escape. The results showed that mRNA release began 3 h after GrAb-LNP incubation, with the majority of mRNA released by 6 h (Figure S8). Next, we investigated whether HER2-induced internalization could facilitate functional mRNA delivery to HER2-positive cancer cells (Figures 2G and S9A). In HER2-positive cell lines (SK-OV-3, SK-BR-3, MDA-MB-453, BT-474), we observed a significant increase in Fluc intensity after treatment with HerLNPs compared to ConLNPs and IsoLNPs. Conversely, in the HER2-negative cell line (MDA-MB-231), there was no detectable increase in Fluc intensity with any of the treatments (Figure S9B). Similar results were obtained using enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) mRNA as an additional reporter. SK-OV-3 cells treated with HerLNPs exhibited higher levels of EGFP expression, as confirmed through fluorescence microscopy (Figure S9C).

Furthermore, p53 mRNA delivery encapsulated in HerLNP (p53@HerLNP) confirmed the restoration of p53 tumor suppressor function and anticancer efficacy in HER2-positive cell lines. For comparison, Fluc mRNA-loaded HerLNPs (Fluc@HerLNP), p53 mRNA-loaded ConLNPs (p53@ConLNP), p53 mRNA-loaded IsoLNPs (p53@IsoLNP) and HerLNPs (p53@HerLNP) were also treated. The results showed that higher p53 expression levels were observed in SK-OV-3 cells treated with p53@HerLNPs compared to other LNPs (Figure 2H). Furthermore, p53@HerLNPs efficiently induced cell death in a dose-dependent manner compared to Fluc@HerLNP, p53@ConLNP, and p53@IsoLNPs in SK-OV-3 cells (Figure 2I). Taken together, these results demonstrate the strong HER2-binding capability of HerLNPs, enabling targeted mRNA delivery to cancer cells expressing HER2 receptors.

sec.title: In Vivo Evaluation of mRNA Delivery by GrAb-LNPs Targeting HER2-Expressing Tumors
sec.p: The in vivo efficacy of GrAb-LNPs for mRNA delivery, designed to actively target tumors via the GrAb, was evaluated in mice bearing HER2-expressing SK-OV-3 tumors. After reaching a tumor volume of 200 mm3, DiD-labeled LNPs containing Fluc mRNA were injected intravenously at a dose of 0.5 mg/kg based on mRNA. Noninvasive near-infrared fluorescence (NIRF) imaging was performed at various time points (1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 h). No significant differences in fluorescence signals were observed between the groups up to 1 h after treatment. However, starting at 3 h, Fluc@HerLNPs showed increased accumulation rates in the targeted tumor tissues, while Fluc@ConLNPs and Fluc@IsoLNPs showed sustained low accumulation rates until the 24 h time point (Figures 3A,B). The strongest fluorescence signal was observed in the Fluc@HerLNP-treated tumor regions at 24 h, representing a 1.9-fold increase compared to Fluc@IsoLNPs. Additionally, pharmacokinetic profiling confirmed that GrAb-LNPs remained in the bloodstream for up to 24 h across all groups, with HerLNP-treated mice maintaining detectable levels of 188.08 ± 48.45 ng/mL (Figure S10). Moreover, no significant differences were observed across any group. This finding suggests that the increased tumor accumulation rates of HerLNPs are not due to the prolonged circulation of HerLNPs, but rather the targeting ability of GrAb. As expected, NIRF imaging of the extracted tumors also showed a significant increase in DiD radiation efficiency and Fluc signal in the HerLNPs (Figures 3C and S11). This ex vivo result illustrates improved Fluc protein expression due to enhanced mRNA@LNP delivery to the target site by the GrAb. Quantitative analysis of homogenized tumor tissues further revealed significantly higher tumor accumulation of Fluc@HerLNPs, with fluorescence and luminescence intensities increasing by 2.7-fold and 5.9-fold, respectively, compared to Fluc@IsoLNPs (Figure 3D). This finding suggests that the targeting ability of GrAb-LNP aligns well with results from other LNP-based tumor targeting studies.13,49,50 Histological assays revealed the strongest signal in the Fluc@HerLNPs, with DiD fluorescence (red color) observed in tumor tissues (Figure 3E). Importantly, DiD fluorescence intensity was significantly decreased in liver tissues of Fluc@HerLNPs compared to other groups, suggesting that trastuzumab-mediated active tumor targeting may reduce off-target effects, particularly in the liver (Figure 3F,G). Quantitative analysis to determine the tumor-to-liver percentages of delivered mRNA revealed significantly higher fluorescence (3.3-fold) and luminescence (7.3-fold) intensities in the Fluc@HerLNPs compared to the Fluc@ConLNPs (Figures 3H and S12). We further assessed the accumulation of GrAb@LNP in tumors across different LP ratios, which varied in the number of attached antibodies (Figure S13). The results demonstrated that GrAb@LNP formulations with lower LP ratios, indicating a higher number of attached antibodies, exhibited both higher tumor accumulation and mRNA delivery efficacy. This finding clearly confirms that the improved tumor-targeting ability was indeed attributable to antibody-mediated targeting. Considering these comprehensive biodistribution results, HerLNPs reconstituted with trastuzumab GrAb demonstrated enhanced mRNA delivery efficacy in tumor tissues via HER2-dependent active targeting, leading to successful translation into target proteins within tumor sites.

sec.title: Therapeutic Efficacy of p53 mRNA Specifically Delivered with Active Targeting GrAb-LNPs
sec.p: The in vivo therapeutic efficacy of HER2-targeting GrAb-LNPs (HerLNPs) for delivery of p53 mRNA was evaluated using an SK-OV-3 xenograft mouse model. Once SK-OV-3 tumor volumes reached approximately 50–80 mm3, treatments were administered intravenously every 3 days for a period of 21 days. The treatments included PBS, Fluc@HerLNPs, p53@ConLNP, and p53@HerLNPs, each at a dose of 0.6 mg/kg based on mRNA (Figure 4A). As expected, the p53@HerLNPs group showed minimal tumor growth over the 21 days compared to the other groups (Figure 4B). On day 21, the tumor volume in the p53@HerLNPs group (108.08 ± 16.28 mm3) was significantly lower than in the PBS (474.26 ± 49.66 mm3), Fluc@HerLNPs (510.44 ± 55.02 mm3), and p53@ConLNP (370.50 ± 117.45 mm3) groups (Figure S14). Photographs and weights of the extracted tumors on day 21 further demonstrated the enhanced antitumor efficacy of p53@HerLNPs, showing a 4.6-fold decrease in tumor weight compared to the p53@ConLNPs group (Figure 4C,D). To confirm that the suppression of tumor growth was due to the delivered p53 mRNA, the expression level of p53 protein in tumor tissues was assessed by Western blot analysis and immunofluorescence staining. Quantification of band intensity revealed a significant upregulation of p53 protein in the p53@HerLNP-treated group compared to the p53@ConLNP group (3.9-fold; Figure 4E). Furthermore, the fluorescence signal of p53 (red) was significantly increased in tumors from mice treated with p53@HerLNPs compared to other groups (Figure 4F).

sec.p: Therapeutic effects were further evaluated by H&E and TUNEL staining of tumor tissues harvested on day 21, which revealed severe apoptotic cell death and structural abnormalities in tumors from mice treated with p53@HerLNPs (Figure 4G). Taken together, these results indicate that delivery of p53 mRNA to HER2-overexpressing cancer cells using HER2-targeting GrAb-LNPs leads to enhanced therapeutic effects in vivo. This is achieved through the specific upregulation of p53 protein within SK-OV-3 tumors, highlighting the potential efficacy of GrAb-LNPs in eliciting antitumor responses via targeted mRNA delivery.

sec.title: In Vivo Safety of the GrAb-LNPs
sec.p: The in vivo safety evaluation of GrAb-LNPs was performed in mice using the same protocol as shown in Figure 4. Over a 21 day observation period, mice treated with HerLNPs (Fluc@HerLNPs and p53@HerLNPs) showed no detectable difference in body weight compared to the PBS-treated group (Figure 5A). In contrast, mice treated with p53@ConLNPs, which lack the HER2 targeting moiety, exhibited significant body weight loss (5.47%) by day 21, indicating off-target toxicity associated with LNP administration.

sec.p: Blood chemistry analysis on day 21 showed that HerLNPs did not induce liver toxicity as evidenced by stable serum aspartate transaminase (AST), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels (Figure 5B). Conversely, p53@ConLNPs-treated mice exhibited severe toxicity with elevated levels of AST (2.0- and 2.4-fold), ALT (2.5- and 2.9-fold), and ALP (1.9- and 2.5-fold) compared to the PBS and p53@HerLNPs groups, respectively. Interestingly, all other toxicity markers in serum and whole blood showed no significant differences among all groups, including p53@ConLNPs (Figure 5C,D). This liver-specific toxicity correlates with the biodistribution results in Figure 4, showing higher LNP accumulation rates in the liver in the absence of the HER2-targeting antibody corona. As expected, histological analysis of the liver showed severe histopathological abnormalities and tissue necrosis exclusively in p53@ConLNP-treated mice, which received naked LNPs lacking antibody modification (Figure 5E). In contrast, HerLNP-treated mice showed no structural damage or toxicity in any of the major organs, including the lung, spleen, kidney, and heart (Figure S15). These results consistently support the potential of GrAb-LNPs as a safe mRNA carrier that effectively mitigates liver-specific toxicity—a known side effect of LNPs—while avoiding any systemic toxicity.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: We have successfully developed GrAb-LNPs, an advanced targeted mRNA delivery platform, by incorporating lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) with engineered antibodies fused to apolipoprotein in the Fc region. Leveraging the strong binding force of ApoA1 for lipid structures (∼200 kCal/mol), the integration of antibodies into LNPs was achieved through a spontaneous and straightforward process, bypassing the need for complex and unstable chemical conjugation methods.38 Unlike traditional chemical approaches, this biomolecule-mediated incorporation technique allows the application of antibodies to any lipid composition without the need for functional group introduction.23

The results demonstrated the superior binding and targeting capabilities of GrAb-LNPs in HER2-overexpressing cancer models both in vitro and in vivo. Specifically, when targeting SK-OV-3 cells, GrAb-LNPs showed a 24.4-fold increase in uptake in vitro, while in vivo studies showed a more modest 2.7-fold increase compared to the IsoLNP group. This reduced in vivo efficacy likely results from physiological challenges that affect antibody binding, such as reduced accessibility to tumor cells and altered receptor engagement in a complex tissue context.51,52 This targeted delivery approach has significantly reduced off-target toxicity, particularly regarding hepatotoxicity, a major barrier to the clinical translation of LNPs as therapeutic carriers. Hepatotoxicity has been a major barrier to the clinical translation of LNPs as therapeutic carriers.53−55 By employing targeting strategies that reduce LNP accumulation in the liver, we achieved lower liver toxicity and improved systemic safety, as confirmed by extensive in vivo safety evaluations, including histological and blood analyses.

Another key advantage of GrAb LNPs is the incorporation of ApoA1 protein around the LNPs, which acts as a protective shield against protein corona formation under biological conditions.56,57 Typically, when LNPs enter the bloodstream, they interact with various proteins, forming a protein corona that leads to opsonization and rapid immune clearance.58,59 Our system mitigates this problem by attaching the dysopsonin protein ApoA1 to LNPs prior to injection, effectively minimizing potential metabolic changes and preventing unwanted immune responses.60,61

Importantly, this advantageous approach is not confined to HER2-targeting; it offers adaptability to target any receptor by modifying the variable region of the antibody. This inherent flexibility opens avenues for broad applications across various diseases beyond ovarian cancers, including lymphoma immunotherapy, vaccine development, and in vivo CAR-T cell engineering. Given the outstanding therapeutic performance, simplicity of the reaction process, and broad applicability, GrAb-LNPs have the potential to advance LNP-based mRNA delivery technology.

sec.title: Gene Synthesis and Cloning
sec.p: Nucleotide sequences were optimized by GeneOptimizer software (Thermo Scientific) and further evaluated with GenScript (Piscataway) to minimize rare codons. Optimized sequences were synthesized by IDT as gBlocks gene fragments. All cloning experiments were performed using a sequence- and ligation-independent cloning method. Insert or vector nucleotides were amplified using KOD Plus Neo DNA Polymerase (TOKOD-401, TOYOBO) and digested with DpnI (R017L, NEB). The insert and vector nucleotides were assembled using T4 DNA polymerase (M0203S, NEB). The resulting plasmids were used to transform E. coli TOP10 hosts and subsequently sequenced.

sec.title: Construction and Production of GrAb
sec.p: A dual vector system was employed to engineer the GrAb constructs for targeting HER2 and control applications. The first vector, IgL, included the coding sequences for the signal peptide, variable light (VL), and constant light (CL) domains. The second vector, IgH, included the signal peptide, constant heavy 1 (CH1), hinge, constant heavy 2 (CH2), constant heavy 3 (CH3) domains, a Gly4Ser linker, and an apolipoprotein fusion segment. The signal peptide sequence utilized across both vectors was MGWSCIILFLVATATGAHS for efficient protein secretion. The backbone of the GrAb was based on human IgG1 to leverage its well-documented biological functions and structural properties.

For HER2 targeting, variable regions from trastuzumab (VH and VL) were integrated into the respective IgL and IgH vectors. The isotype control GrAb employed VH and VL domains from the Foralumab (NI-0401). Apolipoprotein fusion was achieved by incorporating the mature forms of ApoA1 (amino acids 25–267) and ApoE3 (amino acids 19–219).

ExpiCHO-S (A29127, Gibco) cells were used as an expression host to produce the GrAb. The cells were seeded at a density of 6.0 × 106 cells/mL. The following day, cotransfection of the heavy and light chains of the GrAb plasmids was performed using an ExpiFectamine CHO transfection kit (A14524, Invitrogen) as the transfection reagent. The plasmids encoding the heavy and light chains were transfected at a ratio of 1:1, with a total of 1 μg of DNA per culture volume (mL). Transfected cells were cultured at 37 °C with 8% CO2 in a shaking incubator at 120 rpm. After 13 days, supernatants were harvested at 4 °C, 7,000g, 30 min and filtered using a 0.22 μm PES membrane filter. GrAb was purified using a protein A purification system and dialyzed with 1 kDa MWCO dialysis membrane.

sec.title: In Vitro Transcription of mRNA
sec.p: For in vitro transcription, the template was linearized with the HindIII-HF restriction enzyme (R3104L, NEB). mRNA was produced using the Takara IVTpro T7 mRNA Synthesis Kit (6144, Takara) with CleanCap Reagent AG (3′ OMe) (N-7413, Trilink), following the manufacturer’s protocol. The mRNA’s uridine was replaced with N1-Methyl-Pseudouridine (HY-112582A, MCE). The mRNA was purified with Monarch RNA Cleanup Kit (T2040L, NEB), eluted with RNase-free DW (1 μg/μL), and stored at −80 °C until use.

sec.title: Formulation of LNP and Incorporation of GrAb
sec.p: An ethanol solution with a lipid concentration of 6.25 mM was prepared, containing the following components for Con LNPs: SM-102 (CAY10779, Cayman), cholesterol (C8667, Sigma), DSPC (850365C, Avanti), and DMG-PEG2000 (880151P, Avanti) at a molar ratio of 50:38.5:10:1.5. For fluorescent labeling, 1,1′-dioctadecyl-3,3,3′,3′-tetramethylindodicarbocyanine, 4-chlorobenzenesulfonate Salt (DiD, D7757, Invitrogen) were added to the ethanol phase at 1 mol % relative to the total lipid. The aqueous phase containing mRNA was prepared using a 10 mM sodium citrate buffer at pH 3. The ionizable lipid: mRNA amine/phosphate (N/P) ratio was fixed at 6. The volume ratio between ethanol and aqueous phase was adjusted to 1:3. The LNP was diluted 4-fold with PBS (pH 7.4). For the GrAb-LNPs formulation, the LNP mixture and the GrAb protein were mixed at a lipid/protein molar ratio (LP ratio) of 10,000:1, followed by incubation for 30 min at 37 °C. Subsequently, the LNPs and GrAb-LNPs were dialyzed twice with PBS (pH 7.4) using a 1 Mda MWCO centrifugal filter for 10 min at 12,000g and stored at 4 °C.

sec.title: Analysis of the Incorporation Efficiency of GrAb into LNPs
sec.p: To determine the percentage of antibody incorporation on the surface of LNPs in the presence or absence of ApoA1, the antibody and GrAb were labeled via cyanine5 NHS ester (13020, Lumiprobe) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. LNPs and antibody or GrAb were incubated at 37 °C for 30 min at an LP ratio of 10,000:1. Unbound antibodies were then removed using a 1 Mda MWCO centrifugal filter. The fluorescence of the total protein was measured after passing the labeled protein through a 10 kDa MWCO centrifugal filter. The percentage of antibodies incorporated into the LNP was calculated by subtracting the values obtained in 1 MDa (incorporated protein) centrifugal filter from the 10 kDa centrifugal filter (total protein). The incorporation percentage (%) was calculated using the following formula.

sec.title: Analysis of mRNA Encapsulation Efficacy
sec.p: The mRNA encapsulation efficiency was assessed with a Quant-iT RiboGreen RNA assay Kit (R11490, Invitrogen). Briefly, LNPs were subjected to a 20 min incubation with either 1× TE or 1× TE + 1% Triton X-100. After the incubation, RiboGreen reagent was added to each sample, and the fluorescence intensity was measured at excitation/emission wavelengths of 485/520 nm using a GloMax plate reader (Promega). The amount of RNA loaded into the LNPs (internal RNA) was calculated by subtracting the values obtained in 1× TE (free mRNA) from 1× TE + 1% Triton X-100 (total mRNA). The encapsulation (%) was calculated using the following formula.

sec.title: Analysis of the Surface-Bound GrAbs
sec.p: Using a Nanoparticle Tracking Analyzer (NTA, Nanosight NS300, Amesbury, UK), the size and particle number of the LNPs were determined. The protein concentration was quantified with the Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (Pierce Biotechnology, Rockford, IL, USA). To estimate the number of GrAb molecules per single LNP, the measured protein quantity was converted into the number of molecules using Avogadro’s constant (6.022 × 1023 molecules/mol). This total was then divided by the LNP particle count (1.0 × 1010) to determine the average number of GrAb molecules per LNP. This calculation was performed at a lipid-to-protein ratio (LP ratio) of 10,000:1, assuming 100% binding efficiency.

sec.title: Calculation of the Distance between GrAbs on the Surface of LNPs
sec.p: The distance between GrAbs on the surface of an LNP can be determined through a series of calculations. First, the surface area (A) of the LNP is calculated using the formula for the surface area of a sphere, A = 4πr2, where r is the radius of the LNP (, with D being the diameter). The area occupied by each GrAb (AperGrAb) is then obtained by dividing the total surface area (A) by the number of GrAbs (N) present on the LNP surface: . Assuming a hexagonal arrangement of GrAbs, the relationship between the area occupied by each GrAb and the distance sss between adjacent GrAbs is given by . Using this formula, , the distance between GrAbs was calculated.

sec.title: Analysis of the Attachment Stability of GrAb
sec.p: To evaluate the attachment stability of GrAb on LNPs under physiological conditions, GrAb-LNPs were incubated in 100% mouse serum at 37 °C with shaking at 100 rpm. At various time points (6, 12, and 24 h), LNPs were isolated from serum using a 2 h airfuge ultracentrifugation, separating them from serum proteins.

The isolated LNPs were then quantified for total mRNA content using a RiboGreen assay to ensure equal amounts of mRNA for subsequent Western blot analysis. After quantification, equalized samples were subjected to SDS-PAGE, followed by transfer to a PVDF membrane. The presence of GrAb on the LNPs was detected using a human Fc-specific antibody, confirming the stability of the antibody attachment over time in a serum environment.

For in vivo analysis of GrAb attachment stability, LNPs and GrAb proteins were stained with fluorescence agents. LNPs were labeled with the lipophilic fluorescent dye DiO (Thermo Fisher Scientific) to enable fluorescence detection. LNPs were incubated with DiO at a final concentration of 1% (w/w, relative to total lipids) in ethanol for 24 h at room temperature. Separately, GrAb proteins were labeled with Flamma 675-NHS (BioActs) by reacting with the dye at a molar ratio of 15:1 (dye/GrAb) in sodium bicarbonate buffer (pH 8.5) for 2 h at room temperature. Unbound dyes from both reactions were removed using a PD-10 desalting column (Cytiva) equilibrated with PBS. The labeled GrAb-LNPs were injected intravenously, and blood samples were collected at various time points (0, 6, 12, and 24 h). Colocalization of the fluorescence signals was analyzed using flow cytometry.
Counterstained with Hoechst 33342 (H3570, Thermo Scientific), and analyzed using a confocal laser scanning microscope (Leica).

sec.title: In Vitro Cellular Binding and Uptake Assay
sec.p: MDA-MB-231 HER2− cells and SK-OV-3, MDA-MB-453, SK-BR-3, BT-474 HER2+ cells (1 × 106 cells per sample) were incubated with Con, Iso, HerLNPs (400 ng mRNA/mL) in PBS for 30 min at 37 °C. Cells were washed three times with 1 mL of PBS before analysis on CytoFLEX flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter). For a receptor-blocking procedure, cells were preincubated with trastuzumab at 37 °C for 1 h before treatment with the LNPs. The treated cells were then processed identically to the initial assay, including the washing steps and flow cytometry analysis.

Cy5-labeled Fluc-mRNA-loaded Con, Iso, and HerLNPs were prepared to monitor the cellular uptake of the LNPs. SK-OV-3 cells were seeded in 35 mm confocal dishes (SPL) at a density of 5 × 105 cells per well and incubated at 37 °C in 5% CO2 for 24 h. The cells were then incubated with LNPs at different time intervals. After incubation, the cells were washed with PBS, counterstained with Hoechst 33342 (H3570, Thermo Scientific), and analyzed using a confocal laser scanning microscope (Leica).

sec.title: In Vitro mRNA Release Profiling
sec.p: For time-dependent mRNA release profiling, SK-OV-3 cells were treated with 0.1 mg/mL calcein and HerLNPs (400 ng mRNA/mL) at specified time points. After three washes with DPBS and replacement with serum-free DMEM, fluorescence imaging was conducted using a confocal laser scanning microscope. The degree of colocalization was quantified using Pearson’s correlation coefficient.

sec.title: In Vitro Cellular Transfection
sec.p: For Fluc transfection, MDA-MB-231, SK-OV-3, MDA-MB-453, SK-BR-3, and BT-474 cells were seeded in a 48-well plate. After 24 h, cells were treated with Fluc-loaded Con, Iso, and HerLNPs (50 ng of mRNA per well). After 2 h of incubation, the cells were washed with PBS (pH 7.4) and further incubated in a fresh medium for another 24 h. 45 μL of cell culture lysis 5X reagent (CCLR, E1531, Promega) were added and transferred to white 96-well plates. After adding 100 μL of luciferase assay substrate (E1501, Promega) to each well, the resulting luminescence was measured using a GloMax plate reader.

For EGFP transfection, SK-OV-3 cells were seeded in a 6-well plate at a density of 5 × 105 cells per well and incubated at 37 °C in 5% CO2 for 24 h. Subsequently, the cells were visualized using an EVOS M5000 fluorescence microscope (Invitrogen).

sec.title: In Vitro Cell Growth Inhibition Assay
sec.p: SK-OV-3 cells were seeded in 48-well plates at a density of 1 × 104 cells per well. After 24 h to allow cell adherence, cells were treated with PBS, Fluc@HerLNPs, p53@ConLNPs, p53@IsoLNPs, and p53@HerLNPs at various mRNA concentrations (0.125, 0.250, 0.500, and 1.000 and 2.000 μg/mL). After 24 h of incubation, the cells were washed with PBS buffer (pH 7.4) and further incubated in a fresh medium for another 24 h. Cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8, CK-04, Dojindo) was used to verify the in vitro cell growth inhibition efficacy of p53@LNPs.

sec.title: Xenograft Mouse Models
sec.p: Seven-week-old female BALB/c nu/nu mice were bred under pathogen-free conditions at the Korea Institute of Science and Technology (KIST). All experiments involving live animals have adhered to the relevant laws and institutional guidelines of the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at KIST (Approval number: KIST-2022-04-072). For the preparation of xenograft mouse models, 2 × 106 SK-OV-3 cells in the mixture of DMEM (50 μL) and matrigel (50 μL, 354230, Corning) were subcutaneously inoculated into the left flank of the mice.

sec.title: Biodistribution of GrAb-LNPs
sec.p: When the average SK-OV-3 tumor volume reached 200 mm3, DiD-labeled LNPs containing Fluc mRNA (0.5 mg/kg based on mRNA) were intravenously injected into the mice. At specified time points, noninvasive NIRF imaging was conducted using the IVIS Lumina Series III system (PerkinElmer). The tumor tissues and major organs (liver, lung, spleen, kidney, heart) were collected 24 h postinjection for ex vivo fluorescence imaging. For luminescence imaging, organs were soaked in d-luciferin solution (4 mM d-luciferin, 2 mM ATP) in PBS for 5 min. After 5 min incubation, bioluminescence imaging was performed. The fluorescence and luminescence intensities in tumors and each organ were quantified using Living Image software (PerkinElmer). Finally, tumor tissues were harvested, embedded in OCT compound for cryosection, and counterstained with DAPI. The fluorescence image of sectioned tissue was observed using confocal microscopy (Leica).

sec.title: Pharmacokinetic Profiling of GrAb-LNPs
sec.p: The pharmacokinetic (PK) profiles of DiD-labeled GrAb-LNPs were evaluated following intravenous administration. Blood samples were collected from mice at specified time points postinjection (1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 h) through cardiac puncture under deep anesthesia. The samples were then analyzed using a GloMax plate reader.

sec.title: In Vivo Therapeutic Effect of GrAb-LNPs
sec.p: To evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of GrAb-LNPs, the mice were randomly divided into four groups (n = 5) on day 7 after subcutaneous injection of SK-OV-3 cells. Subsequently, PBS, Fluc@HerLNPs, p53@ConLNPs, and p53@HerLNPs (0.6 mg/kg based on mRNA) were intravenously administered 5 times, with a 3 day interval. Tumor volume and body weights were measured every 2 days, wherein tumor dimensions were measured with calipers, and tumor volume was calculated as 0.5 × (width)2 × (length)2. On day 21, the mice were euthanized, and the tumors, organs, and blood were collected for further experiments.

sec.title: Histological Analysis of Tumor Tissue
sec.p: For the histological analysis of extracted tumor tissue, tumors were fixed in a 4% paraformaldehyde solution. Following this, tumors were embedded in paraffin and sectioned to a thickness of 5 μm using a rotary microtome. The resulting sections underwent staining procedures, including hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase-mediated deoxyuridine triphosphate nick end labeling (TUNEL) staining. To assess the p53 protein level in tumor tissue, the deparaffinized and rehydrated sections underwent 24 h incubation with a p53 antibody (DO-1, Santa Cruz). Subsequently, following incubation with a FITC-conjugated rabbit anti-mouse secondary antibody and DAPI for 1 h and 10 min, respectively, fluorescence images were observed using a confocal laser scanning microscope (Leica).

sec.title: In Vivo Toxicity Test
sec.p: To evaluate the in vivo toxicity, the harvested organs, including the liver, lung, spleen, kidney, and heart, underwent fixation with 4% PFA and subsequent embedding in paraffin. Following this, tissues were sectioned with a thickness of 5 μm and subjected to H&E staining. For serum biochemical analysis, blood samples were centrifuged at 1,200 rpm for 20 min, and supernatants were obtained. The comprehensive analysis of both whole blood and serum components was conducted by DKKOREA CO., Ltd.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Statistical significance between the two groups was analyzed using the Student’s t-test. For comparisons involving more than two groups, we utilized a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by multiple comparisons employing the Tukey–Kramer posthoc test. All results are presented as mean ± SD, and P values of >0.05n.s., <0.05*, <0.01**, 0.001***, and <0.0001**** were considered statistically significant.
